title: When prayer feels empty
hookLine: you pray and feel nothing; the Psalms have a name and a picture for it

lines: THE BIBLE HAS A PICTURE FOR IT.
cards: Ten seconds in, the mind has already wandered off: the email, the thing someone said at lunch. You bring it back. You say the words.
And it feels like talking into a phone after the call has quietly dropped. Nothing on the other end. Not anger.
Not exactly doubt. Just nothing. On Christian forums people confess this again and again: prayer feels empty, even fake, and they wonder what's wrong with them.
The Bible's own prayer book has a picture for exactly this, and it's spoken to God, not about him.

teach.b: Dryness. Christian writers have used that word for centuries for prayer that feels like nothing. The picture comes from the Psalms.
One prays, in the King James Bible: "my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is."
Another, from someone far from the temple, says: "My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God," while people keep asking, "Where is thy God?" So the feeling isn't a modern failure.

It sits in the Bible's prayer book, prayed by people who kept praying. Catholic and Orthodox spiritual writers teach that dryness comes and goes; later on this path you'll meet John of the Cross and his dark night.
Many evangelical pastors call it a dry season. C. S.
Lewis wrote a book of letters from a senior devil to a junior one, and the devil admits what worries him most: a person who feels nothing, still intends to do God's will, and keeps going.
So what do people do in a dry stretch? Keep it small: one honest sentence.

Borrow words, a psalm or the Lord's Prayer, when your own run out. Tell someone: a pastor, a priest, a friend who prays. And look at the rest of life, because sleep, grief and stress all dry the ground.
If the flatness isn't only in prayer, if food, friends and the things you love have gone gray too, that can be depression.

It's an illness, not a failure of faith, and seeing a doctor or a counselor isn't a lack of faith either. If you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: Many Christians go through dry seasons in prayer. Priests, pastors and spiritual directors commonly suggest keeping prayer short and honest, leaning on set prayers like the Psalms, and talking it over with someone they trust.

o: a strict fast from water on holy days
a cold faith that has given up on God
a stretch when prayer feels empty or flat

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a psalm's picture of longing for God
what people kept asking the psalmist
an illness, not a failure of faith

s: feeling nothing in prayer means you're doing it wrong
the Psalms pray from "a dry and thirsty land." people in the Bible kept praying through it.
in C. S. Lewis's book, the devil worries about someone who keeps going without feeling
a person who feels nothing and still intends to do God's will is the one the devil fears.
seeing a doctor or counselor shows a lack of faith
depression is an illness. getting help isn't a failure of faith.

games.q: for weeks, prayer has felt like talking to an empty room. a friend who prays asks how it's going. what do you do?
o: tell the truth: it feels dry right now.
stop praying until the feeling comes back.
games.why: the Psalms tell the truth out loud: "my soul thirsteth." dryness said honestly is still prayer, and a friend can help carry it.

practice: Don't try to feel anything. If you pray, say one honest sentence, maybe the psalm's own, my soul thirsteth, or simply, I don't feel you, and I'm here anyway, then stay and let nothing happen.
If you don't pray, just sit, and notice that showing up still counts when it's quiet.

wordCard.voice: Dryness: the old Christian name for prayer that feels like nothing, pictured in the Psalms as a dry and thirsty land.

orig.note: Hebrew: dry land, drought. the word behind "dry" in Psalm 63:1.

carryVoice: Your line: a dry prayer still counts. If prayer feels empty today, one honest sentence is enough. Day one hundred six.
